source.title: Interpolation under latent factor regression models
source.authors: F. Bunea; Seth Strimas-Mackey; M. Wegkamp

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present. The title in the text differs from the supplied title, but the arXiv identifier matches.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures prediction risk across a feature-dimension-to-sample-size ratio in minimum-norm regression simulations, testing for a double-descent pattern with a method different from deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The risk curves in Figures 1, 2 and 4 are relevant results. The stated comparisons that LASSO and PCR outperform GLS in a sparse setting are risk rankings, not results about the claimed curve shape, so they are not separate rows. The null predictor is shown as a reference but does not test the curve shape.
record.test_reason: The study reports theory and simulations of min-norm least-squares risk against p/n in a latent factor regression model, a non-deep model class. It explicitly reports a risk peak at p/n = 1, a second descent toward zero, and no peak for regularized predictors. This bears on V4 and on the regularization part of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but incomplete. The authors' main results are finite-sample risk bounds. When the effective rank of Sigma_X is much larger than n, the min-norm interpolator's risk approaches the null risk. Under a factor regression model with effective rank below n (while p >> n), its excess risk can go to zero and is comparable to PCR and Ridge, and can beat LASSO. In simulation, the GLS risk peaks at p/n = 1, and the regularized methods show no peak there.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes minimum-norm least-squares prediction under a latent factor regression model and plots simulated risk against p/n; it is not a deep-network replication.
record.method_sensitivity: The plotted outcomes vary with predictor choice and with the simulated factor/loading configuration, including the sparse setting in Figure 4. LASSO and Ridge tuning parameters are chosen by cross-validation.
record.problems: The reported curve values are presented in plots without extracted numerical coordinates or uncertainty bars. The explicit peak description is for one simulated setting; other plotted settings are described less fully.
record.rows_left_out: The null predictor is plotted as a reference, but its risk does not test the curve shape. Figure 4 also compares method risk levels, including LASSO and PCR outperforming GLS in the sparse setting; that ranking does not bear on the listed curve claims.

untested.parts: All: n is not varied at fixed p.
All: no effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Whether label noise or variance drives the peak; whether multiple peaks occur; whether tuning is truly optimal.

missing.what: Theorem 1: when effective rank re(Sigma_X) >> n, R(alpha-hat)/R(0) approaches 1, so the interpolator's risk approaches null risk.
Theorem 13 and Corollary 14: finite-sample bound showing min-norm excess risk goes to zero for p >> n under the factor model (theoretical second descent).
Ridge (CV-tuned) risk approaches the GLS risk for p >> n, suggesting the optimal ridge penalty goes to zero far past the threshold.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The p/n axis changes n, p and K jointly (n = floor(K^1.5)), so it is not a pure capacity sweep. All curve evidence is figure-only, with no uncertainty reported. The sparse-setting risk rankings in Figure 4 are correctly left out as rows.

versions.untested_parts: Deep networks and model-size scaling in deep networks.
Changing the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
Other model classes beyond the studied minimum-norm factor-regression setting.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs and sample count.

Whether label noise or variance drives the peak; whether multiple or triple descent occurs; whether the peak disappears under optimally tuned regularization. The study compares regularized predictors, but does not establish that their tuning is optimal.
Whether counting effective parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: Min-norm least squares (GLS) under factor regression simulations (Figures 1, 2, 4)
relationships.reason: Excess risk peaks at p/n = 1 (r2) and descends toward zero as p/n grows past 1 in all three settings (r1, r2, r6).
relationships.display_finding: Excess risk peaked at p/n=1 and declined toward zero as p/n increased beyond 1 in all three simulated settings.

relationships.condition: Min-norm interpolator when the effective rank of Sigma_X is much larger than n (e.g. well-conditioned features)
relationships.reason: Theorem 1 (text, no row) shows the risk then approaches the trivial null risk R(0). A beneficial second descent needs jointly low-dimensional (X, y) structure.
relationships.display_finding: Risk approached the null predictor's risk R(0), making beneficial recovery dependent on jointly low-dimensional structure in features and targets.

relationships.condition: Regularized predictors (oracle-K PCR, CV-tuned LASSO and Ridge) in the Figure 2 setting
relationships.reason: The text says the peak at p/n = 1 is absent for PCR, LASSO and Ridge because they are regularized there (r3-r5). Tuning is cross-validated, not proven optimal.
relationships.display_finding: The peak at p/n = 1 was absent for oracle-K PCR and cross-validated LASSO and ridge.
